3	Multi-judge panels are widely deployed for robust Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation, yet adding judges can shift, not reduce, the dominant vulnerability pathway. Existing defenses conflate panel diversity with individual judge robustness, and it remains unclear which factor drives attack success rate (ASR) reduction. We decompose panel ASR into weakest-link susceptibility ($\eta_{\max}$) and effective independent channels ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) across 15 models, six attack types, two benchmarks, and panel sizes $K \in \{3, 5, 7\}$ (up to 6,435 panels). $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$'s coefficient is positive in all 12 conditions under ordinary least squares, but significance varies across inference methods (0 to 12 of 12), and the diversity--capability confound ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$) limits causal claims. The dominant predictor shifts with panel size: at $K{=}3$, both $\eta_{\max}$ and $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ contribute; at $K{\geq}5$, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ dominates while $\eta_{\max}$ attenuates. Aggregation rules modulate predictability ($R^2$: threshold 0.83, Bayesian 0.09). Small panels benefit most from individual robustness screening; larger panels require attention to judge independence.

Multi-judge panels are widely used to defend Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation against manipulation, yet no existing work disentangles whether robustness gains stem from individual judge quality or inter-judge diversity. We decompose panel attack success rate into weakest-link susceptibility ($\eta_{\max}$) and effective independence ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) across 15 models, six attack types, two multiple-choice benchmarks, and panel sizes $K \in \{3, 5, 7\}$ (up to 6,435 panels). Two findings are robust across diversity metrics and inference methods: (1)~diversity is uniformly positively associated with vulnerability (both $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $\kappa$-diversity confirm positive direction in 12/12 conditions), and (2)~$\eta_{\max}$'s predictive power diminishes monotonically with panel size (meta-analytic pooled $\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$: $0.264 \to 0.101 \to 0.084$; confidence interval crosses zero at $K{=}7$). Monte Carlo calibration confirms the wild cluster bootstrap is conservative (max null rejection $1.6\%$ at $\alpha{=}5\%$). Aggregation rules modulate predictability ($R^2$: threshold 0.83, Bayesian 0.09). The diversity--capability confound ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$) precludes causal claims; all findings are associational.

We address this gap by decomposing panel vulnerability into two predictors: weakest-link susceptibility ($\eta_{\max}$, the maximum individual attack success rate in a panel) and effective independent channels ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$, a spectral measure of judge independence). Across all 12 conditions (two benchmarks $\times$ six attacks), $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$'s ordinary least-squares (OLS) coefficient is positive (12/12), directionally consistent with adversarial ensemble theory \citep{goodfellow2015adversarial,papernot2016transferability}. However, the significance of this association is method-sensitive (0 to 12 of 12 across inference approaches), and a previously uncharacterized transition emerges: at $K{=}3$, both predictors contribute (bootstrap significance: $\eta_{\max}$ 3/12, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ 4/12); at $K{\geq}5$, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ becomes the dominant predictor (7/12 at $K{=}5$, 8/12 at $K{=}7$) while $\eta_{\max}$ sharply attenuates (2/12, then 1/12).

Controlled experiments across 15 models (9 API, 6 local quantized), $K \in \{3,5,7\}$, six attack types, and two benchmarks, Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) and the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC), confirm this predictor shift. Under random faults, panel composition is highly predictive ($R^2 = 0.73$--$0.81$); adaptive attack reduces predictability to $R^2 = 0.256$ (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}).

These findings yield three contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Diversity--vulnerability association.} $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$'s coefficient direction is positive in all 12 conditions (12/12 under OLS and generalized additive model (GAM) bootstrap), but the diversity--capability confound ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$) limits causal interpretation: Cinelli--Hazlett robustness values do not exceed the confound in 69\% of conditions (25/36), though fractional logit confirms the positive association (9/12 across all $K$) (\S\ref{sec:dominance}, \S\ref{sec:gam_taxonomy}).
\item \textbf{Panel-size-dependent predictor shift.} At $K{=}3$, both $\eta_{\max}$ (3/12) and $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (4/12) contribute under bootstrap (co-determination); at $K{\geq}5$, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ becomes the dominant predictor (7/12 at $K{=}5$, 8/12 at $K{=}7$) while $\eta_{\max}$ sharply attenuates (2/12, then 1/12) (\S\ref{sec:cross_k}, \S\ref{sec:rf_contrast}).
\item \textbf{Aggregation as predictability control.} Aggregation rules modulate how much variance panel composition explains ($R^2$: threshold 0.83, Bayesian 0.09). Bayesian calibration attenuates $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (5+/1$-$) but $\eta_{\max}$ persists (9/12), so the defense is partial rather than complete (\S\ref{sec:aggregation}, \S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{enumerate}

Our findings are descriptive; the diversity--capability confound ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$; \S\ref{sec:analysis}) limits causal claims.

tool_args.new_string:
\section{Conclusion}

We find that the weakest link diminishes: $\eta_{\max}$'s predictive power declines monotonically from $K{=}3$ to $K{=}7$ (meta-analytic pooled $\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$: $0.264 \to 0.101 \to 0.084$; CI crosses zero at $K{=}7$), while diversity remains uniformly positively associated with vulnerability (both $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $\kappa$-diversity confirm positive direction in 12/12 conditions, pooled CI excluding zero). The diversity significance trajectory, however, is operationalization-dependent ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$: $3 \to 7 \to 8$/12; $\kappa$-diversity: $8 \to 7 \to 6$/12), making it unsuitable as a standalone contribution. Monte Carlo calibration confirms that the wild cluster bootstrap is conservative (max null rejection $1.6\%$), so reported significance counts are lower bounds.

For practitioners, these results suggest a two-regime strategy: at small panel sizes ($K{=}3$), screening for individual judge robustness ($\eta_{\max}$) remains the primary defense; at $K{\geq}5$, panel composition becomes more predictive than individual weakness. The diversity--capability confound ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$; Cinelli--Hazlett RV insufficient in 69\% of conditions) is itself a finding: in current LLM ecosystems, diverse panels are structurally more capable, precluding observational separation.

As model capabilities converge across providers, the confound may weaken, enabling cleaner identification. Future work should pursue capability-controlled designs---training judges to decouple diversity from capability---and extend to open-ended generation benchmarks where the discrete multiple-choice structure does not constrain the attack surface.

\paragraph{Metric Sensitivity of the Diversity Trajectory.}
The diversity significance trajectory depends on operationalization: $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ significance increases with $K$ ($3 \to 7 \to 8$/12), while $\kappa$-diversity \citep{kuncheva2003measures} decreases ($8 \to 7 \to 6$/12; Appendix~\ref{app:alt_diversity}). The $\eta_{\max}$ decline, by contrast, holds under both $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $\kappa$-diversity specifications, making it the more robust finding.
